first.rain: Wipe your feet. Paper hates rain more than I do.
first.snow: Shut the door, quick. Snow’s worse than rain: it waits till it’s inside before it gets anything wet.
first.night: We’re shut, officially. But you came in through the back of a page, so I suppose you’d better have a look round.
first.sunday: It’s Sunday, I’m not open. I come in to read where nobody wants anything from me. Present company excepted.
first.monday: Monday morning. Shops here don’t open till the afternoon, and in forty-odd years nobody’s given me a reason to change that.
first.morning: The kettle’s only just on. Look round all you like, but don’t expect conversation till it’s boiled.
first.evening: I shut at six, in theory. In practice I shut when I get to the end of my chapter.
first.day: Come in, shut the door, it’s not a church. Ask if you’re looking for something. Don’t ask for the one with the blue cover.

again: People think a pencil note spoils a book. It’s the only proof anyone read it.
The price is in pencil, first page, top right. If it’s in pen, it came from a shop that didn’t deserve it.
Everyone wants the book they had when they were twelve. It’s never as good. They always buy it.
The ones on the shelf behind me aren’t for sale. They have the best margins.
You find things in them. Bus tickets, a pressed flower, a letter nobody posted. I keep the letters in a tin. I haven’t read them all.
Last week a man wanted the one with the blue cover, with a lighthouse in it. It was green, and a windmill. We found it.
I’ve had this shop since 1979. I’ve read the ones that matter, and a great many that don’t.
kept: Take one down, then. You read it here, not on the street. And don’t you write in it.
